extracted.intended_audience: Title IX coordinators, K-12 and higher education administrators, institutional legal counsel, compliance officers, and other recipients of Department of Education funding
extracted.subtask_description: Preamble guidance and explanatory discussion of how the Department defines and expects recipients to apply key Title IX regulatory terms (e.g., domestic violence, stalking, relevant, remedies, respondent, student). Responds to public comments and explains implementation, cross-references, and training implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Domestic Violence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department did not incorporate all language from VAWA 2022 into the Title IX definition of domestic violence (notably omitting the VAWA phrase beginning 'in the case of victim services') and removed the modifying words 'of violence' from 'felony and misdemeanor crimes' to more closely align with VAWA 2022; the definition continues to refer to crimes and includes the phrase 'under the family or domestic violence laws of the jurisdiction of the recipient.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omission of the VAWA victim-services language is not a substantive change for Title IX and was intended to avoid confusion since 'victim services' in VAWA refers to services not provided under Title IX. Conduct described in omitted language (e.g., physical or sexual abuse, patterns of coercive behavior including verbal, psychological, economic, or technological abuse) may nevertheless constitute sex-based harassment depending on facts and whether it meets hostile environment or other sex-based harassment elements. Recipients may comply with the Title IX definition and, where applicable, other Federal agency definitions (e.g., HUD). The individual implementing Title IX should be familiar with relevant criminal laws (as they are familiar for Clery Act duties) and recipients may include relevant crimes/definitions in training on scope of sex discrimination. The Department declined to remove the jurisdictional criminal-law reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Stalking
rubrics_metrics.description: Stalking is maintained consistent with VAWA 2022 and the 2020 amendments: 'a course of conduct directed at a specific person that would cause a reasonable person to either fear for their safety or the safety of others or suffer substantial emotional distress.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declined to add examples to the regulation itself but discusses elements: 'course of conduct' requires more than one incident, must be directed at a specific person; stalking may occur in-person or using technology; duration, frequency, and intensity matter. Examples of tactics include watching, following, tracking devices, monitoring online activity, unwanted contact, property invasion, hacking, threats, violence, sabotage, and attacks. The 'reasonable person' standard is a reasonable person in the complainant's position (consistent with Clery Act definitions). 'Substantial emotional distress' need not require medical/professional treatment or counseling. The Department rejects vagueness/overbreadth concerns and notes recipients must consider disability/cultural context and comply with Section 504, the ADA, and Title VI; if a party is a student with a disability, coordinators should consult appropriate IEP/team or disability support offices as provided in §106.8(e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'Relevant' (evidence and questions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Retains the proposed definition: relevant evidence is evidence that is related to allegations of sex discrimination and may aid a decisionmaker in determining whether alleged sex discrimination occurred; relevant questions are those related to the allegations and that may aid in showing whether alleged sex discrimination occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declined to adopt the Federal Rules of Evidence definition or to substitute 'information' for 'evidence.' The definition is intended to be sufficiently broad to include evidence related to allegations and that will aid the decisionmaker but excludes questions/evidence that are related yet would not aid determination. The Department declined to adopt a rule that all evidence that aids credibility is per se relevant; credibility evidence may be relevant only to the extent credibility is in dispute and relevant to allegations (§§106.45(g), 106.46(f)). For access to evidence, recipients must provide parties access to either the relevant and not otherwise impermissible evidence or the same written investigative report that accurately summarizes this evidence; if a postsecondary institution provides access via an investigative report, it must, upon request, provide equal opportunity to access the relevant evidence. The Department declined to provide exhaustive examples since relevance is fact-specific and declined to require a single set of evidentiary rules, leaving recipients flexibility to tailor rules while providing clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Remedies are defined consistently with the 2020 amendments as measures designed to restore or preserve access to the recipient's education program or activity for a particular complainant or other person or group of persons; remedies are individualized and highly fact-specific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because remedies are fact-specific, the definition does not categorically define what a remedy looks like or specify when effects are 'remedied.' The Department provided a non-exhaustive list of possible measures (from the July 2022 NPRM): campus escorts, allowing parking in teachers' lots, schedule and extracurricular changes to separate parties, housing adjustments, medical support and counseling, academic resources/support, reviewing disciplinary actions for causal connection, reimbursement for counseling, tuition adjustments, and other appropriate measures. The Department declined to adopt suggested language to identify entitled persons beyond existing §106.45(h)(3); remedies may be provided, as appropriate, to complainants and other persons the recipient identifies as having had equal access limited or denied by sex discrimination. Remedies are distinct from disciplinary sanctions (the latter may be imposed on respondents). The Department added 'their' to the definition for clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Respondent
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent is retained as a person in their individual capacity; only an individual (not a group or organization) is a respondent in Title IX grievance procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department will not require recipients to apply Title IX grievance procedures to groups or organizations; institutions may address student organizations or entities via applicable codes of conduct. The Department acknowledged concerns about including volunteers as respondents but declined to change the definition, finding the civil-rights protection benefits justify any such recruitment/retention costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'Student With a Disability'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department retained a definition of 'student with a disability' to clarify the intersection of Title IX obligations with obligations to students with disabilities (relevant to §§106.8(e) and 106.44(g)(6)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declined to add an ADA cross-reference (redundant) or to change terminology (e.g., to 'disabled person'), keeping the familiar phrase 'student with a disability.' Questions about application to particular populations are fact-specific and must be decided case-by-case. The definition is intended to strengthen enforcement by clarifying recipient responsibilities toward students with disabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'Title IX'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department revised the definition of 'Title IX' to include 20 U.S.C. 1689 following the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2022 directing establishment of an interagency task force on sexual violence in education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This change updates the list of sections in Title 20 that comprise Title IX to reflect the codified interagency task force provision; no additional procedural guidance provided in this section beyond historical/legal context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'Employee' (left unamended)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declined to add a regulatory definition of 'employee.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because employment arrangements vary across recipients and state employment laws differ, recipients are best positioned to determine who qualifies as an 'employee' for reporting (§106.44(c)) and training (§106.8(d)) obligations. The preamble points readers to the discussion in those sections for additional context on who is subject to employee reporting/training requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'Federal Financial Assistance' (left unamended)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department elected not to amend the definition despite comments raising issues about whether tax-exempt status under 26 U.S.C. 501(c)(3) constitutes Federal financial assistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble explains that tax benefits, exemptions, deductions, and most tax credits are generally not included in statutory/regulatory definitions of Federal financial assistance and that most courts view typical tax benefits as non-contractual and therefore not Federal financial assistance. The Department notes that its Title IX regulations apply only to recipients of Department funding (34 CFR 100.2 incorporated through 34 CFR 106.81); whether tax-exempt status might be considered Federal financial assistance by some courts is outside the scope of these regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'Program or Activity' (left unamended)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declined to amend the current definition of 'program or activity,' finding it consistent with the Civil Rights Restoration Act of 1987 and statutory meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'education program or activity' is not separately defined in Title IX and requires a fact-specific inquiry to determine whether a program or activity of a non-educational institution is educational and thus covered. The preamble notes that if any part of an educational institution receives Federal funds, all of its operations are covered by Title IX (citing case law). The Department rejected narrowing the definition to only elementary/secondary or postsecondary-specific programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'Recipient' (left unamended)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department retained the longstanding definition of 'recipient' and declined to amend it despite comments invoking the Fourth Circuit's Peltier v. Charter Day School decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department agrees with the Fourth Circuit that entities receiving federal assistance directly or through an intermediary (e.g., charter school operating companies or subcontractors) are 'recipients' within Title IX's meaning and therefore declines to amend the definition. The preamble cites case law (NCAA v. Smith) to support that entities receiving federal assistance through an intermediary fall within 'recipient.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'Student' (longstanding definition retained)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department retained the longstanding regulatory definition of 'student' as 'a person who has gained admission' (in effect since 1975).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department rejected suggestions to change to an 'in attendance' or 'enrolled' formulation (e.g., FERPA or Clery phrasing). The preamble explains that recipients have been required to notify students (including admitted applicants) of nondiscrimination policies and resolve student complaints since 1975; Title IX protects applicants and admitted students and recipients must provide appropriate access to policies and procedures. Concerns about burdens of notifying all admitted students were discussed but the Department found the longstanding practice appropriate.
